BEYOND EARTH: Archive of Forgotten Space Explorers

What Does It Do and How Does It Work? BEYOND EARTH is an interactive digital storybook and archival web exhibition that documents the machines, laboratories, and personal keepsakes humanity has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Rather than presenting users with a dense, overwhelming spreadsheet of mission telemetry, our web application organizes over fifty years of planetary exploration into an accessible, two-volume reading experience:

  • Overview Portal: Introduces the philosophy of off-world hardware through a four-part visual narrative and six curated "Archival Field Notes" before inviting users to select a destination volume.
  • Volume I — The Moon (5 Chapters): Guides readers through the six Apollo Lunar Module Descent Stages left behind as launchpads, the three electric Lunar Roving Vehicles parked to film liftoff, the nuclear-powered ALSEP laboratories that recorded over 12,000 moonquakes, the passive Lunar Laser Retroreflectors still reflecting Earth lasers today, and personal astronaut mementos like Charlie Duke’s family portrait and Alan Shepard’s golf balls.
  • Volume II — Mars (7 Chapters): Traces the chronological story of robotic pioneers across the Red Planet—from Mariner 9 (1971) and the Viking 1 & 2 Landers (1976) to the Sojourner Rover (1997), Spirit & Opportunity (2004), the Phoenix Arctic Lander (2008), the InSight Seismometer Lander (2018), and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter (2021–2024).
  • Interactive Chapter Workspace & Lightbox: Each volume features a sticky left-hand chapter sidebar that tracks reading progress in real time ("Pending" vs. "Read"). Every chapter pairs a centered, click-to-zoom official NASA archival photograph (with a fullscreen lightbox modal) alongside accessible book-style prose, a point-wise Chapter Summary, and Archival Field Notes & Fun Facts.
  • Mastery-Gated Assessment & Honour Roll: To ensure genuine learning, our 10-question Space Archive Assessment Quiz remains locked ([Locked]) until the user completes all 5 Moon chapters and all 7 Mars chapters. Once unlocked, readers test their knowledge, earn a historian designation (such as Chief Archival Historian), and log their name onto a persistent Archive Honour Roll leaderboard.

What Benefits Does It Have and What Is the Intended Impact?

  • Bridging the Science-to-Student Gap: Official NASA archives (such as the NSSDCA and Planetary Photojournal) contain extraordinary history, but their technical terminology often intimidates younger students and casual learners. BEYOND EARTH translates complex aerospace engineering—such as the Rocket Equation, corner-cube prism optics, and radioisotope thermoelectric power—into warm, engaging stories that any school-age student can immediately grasp and enjoy.
  • Reframing "Space Debris" as Human Heritage: Our intended impact is to shift how the public views inactive spacecraft. Instead of seeing silent rovers and descent stages as abandoned scrap metal, readers discover how these machines sacrificed themselves for safe landings, unlocked the history of water in our solar system, and continue to serve science today (such as Apollo's passive laser mirrors proving the Moon drifts away by 3.8 cm every year, or Ingenuity waking up daily to log Martian weather).
  • Ready for Classrooms & Museums: Because the application requires zero installation, accounts, or backend servers, teachers and students anywhere in the world can open it instantly in any web browser as a self-paced planetary history lesson.

How Is Our Project Creative?

  1. First-Person Machine Monologues ("Voices of the Machines"): Every chapter begins with an empathetic, first-person diary quote written from the perspective of the hardware itself—giving a voice to the Apollo 11 Eagle Descent Stage, the Little Sojourner Rover, and the Ingenuity Helicopter.
  2. Bespoke Archival Editorial Aesthetic: Moving away from generic sci-fi neon interfaces, we designed a museum-grade editorial interface using warm obsidian and parchment tones, classical serif drop-caps (Playfair Display), and technical monospace metadata (JetBrains Mono) that makes the website feel like an authentic, illustrated space-history tome.
  3. Mastery-Locked Gamification: Instead of allowing users to click randomly through a trivia game, we tied the quiz directly to the reading state of both volumes. Watching the navigation status dots turn green and unlocking the final assessment gives students a tangible sense of accomplishment.
  4. Self-Healing Offline SVG Plate Generator: To guarantee reliability during live demos or in classrooms with restricted Wi-Fi, we wrote a custom JavaScript function (buildSvgFallback) that automatically generates a high-resolution vector technical blueprint plate if any external photograph fails to load.

What Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Did We Use?

  • Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3 (utilizing CSS Custom Properties, CSS Grid, Flexbox, backdrop-filter glassmorphism, and responsive media queries), and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+ DOM manipulation, Set state tracking, and localStorage persistence).
  • Graphics & Typography: Dynamic inline SVG vector generation for offline technical plate fallbacks, and open-source Google Fonts (Playfair Display, Plus Jakarta Sans, and JetBrains Mono).
  • NASA Data & Archival Sources: Official public-domain imagery and mission telemetry from the NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov), JPL Planetary Photojournal (PIA series), NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (AS series).

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Readability & Cognitive Load: Early iterations of our project included dense technical specs and complex sliders. After reviewing our target audience of students and space enthusiasts, we intentionally simplified the prose into a clean storybook format and added bulleted Chapter Summaries at the bottom of every page so key scientific takeaways are never missed.
  • Scope & Relevance: We strictly focused our content on The Moon and Mars—removing deep-space probes—to directly honor the challenge prompt and give full narrative depth to 12 landmark lunar and Martian missions.
  • Network Resilience & Zero Dependencies: By packaging the entire application into a lightweight, single-file architecture with built-in SVG image fallbacks and local storage, we ensured fast load times, zero external library failures, and smooth performance across both desktop and mobile devices.
